At the harbor gate, Mira spotted a blue coat across the quay. Her uncle owned a coat exactly that color, and the man inside this one had raised his arm. She waved enthusiastically. He waved again, more urgently. Mira answered with both hands.
Then she noticed that his eyes were fixed above her head. A crane was lowering a cargo net behind her, and the man was directing its operator. His gestures had nothing to do with her greeting. She lowered one hand and converted the other into an elaborate stretch, as if loosening her shoulder had been her intention all along.
The man brought his palm down. The net settled. Mira, who had now stretched enough to prepare for a swimming race, inspected the timetable with extraordinary concentration. questions.prompt: According to the passage, under which condition does light change direction at the water-air boundary?

choices.A: It crosses the boundary at an angle rather than straight on.
choices.B: It remains entirely within the straw.
choices.C: Its speed stays unchanged in the two materials.
choices.D: The observer first removes the straw from the glass.

questions.correctAnswer: It crosses the boundary at an angle rather than straight on.
questions.explanation: The explanation explicitly links the change in direction to crossing at an angle and contrasts this with crossing straight on.
questions.stimulusText:
Put a straight straw into a clear glass of water and look at it from the side at an angle. The straw may seem to bend where it enters the water. Remove it, however, and it is as straight as before. The change is in the light reaching your eyes, not in the straw.
Light travels at different speeds through water and air. When it crosses the boundary at an angle, its direction changes. This bending of the light is called refraction. Light from the submerged section follows a different route to your eye from light coming from the part above the surface. Your visual system interprets the arriving light as though it had traveled in straight lines, placing the underwater section at an apparent position different from its actual one.
Viewing direction matters. Light crossing the boundary straight on does not change direction there, even though its speed changes. Thus, a change in speed does not always produce an apparent bend.
The demonstration separates an object from its appearance. Looking at the straw after removing it provides a check: the apparent bend disappears without any straightening force being applied. A report about where an object seems to be must therefore include how the observer is looking at it.

questions.stimulusTitle: A Copy With Its Own Job
questions.stimulusText:
Imagine an ancient coin whose worn design is difficult to see. A maker produces a clearly marked replica with sharper raised lines. Visitors can handle the replica, turn it toward a lamp, and discover a figure that is hard to recognize on the original. The copy may be easier to study in this particular way. It has not, however, become the ancient coin.
The distinction concerns history as well as appearance. Marks on the original may record its use, the material available to its maker, or later damage. Marks deliberately added to a new replica demonstrate what the modern maker chose to reproduce. Even a very accurate copy cannot acquire the earlier object's actual journey merely by resembling it.
This does not make copying a worthless activity. A replica answers some questions while leaving others to the original. It can help explain the arrangement of a design, permit handling, or show a proposed reconstruction. A label should say which of these jobs it performs and where the reconstruction involves uncertainty.
Calling a replica a replacement is therefore like calling a rehearsal the performance that already happened. A rehearsal may reveal how an action could have been carried out; it does not become that earlier event. The useful question is not simply whether a copy is good, but what it is good for.

questions.stimulusText:
"Just slide your hand across," I told Sami. "The pen will follow."
My cousin tried. A blue streak appeared below the sentence, where the side of his left hand had passed through the wet ink. I pushed a clean sheet toward him and demonstrated again with my right hand.
"Just keep your hand here."
He looked from my fingers to his own. "That is where mine was."
I was about to repeat the demonstration when he turned the paper to a different angle. He wrote his name slowly. This time his hand crossed less of the fresh writing, and the letters remained clear. He shifted the sheet a little more and tried again.
I had prepared a whole explanation about smooth strokes and graceful curves. It suddenly seemed that I had been describing what my hand already knew, without looking at what his hand was doing.
"Could you show me that angle?" I asked.
Sami turned the page back and repeated the movement. I watched the space between the nib and his wrist instead of watching my own example. Then we tested another sheet together.
On the instruction card I had made, the first line began, "Just hold the pen naturally." I crossed out Just. After a moment, I crossed out naturally too. There was room below for a more useful beginning.

questions.stimulusTitle: Why a Full Moon Usually Stays Bright
questions.stimulusText:
A full Moon and a lunar eclipse are related, but they are not the same event. At full Moon, we see the Moon's sunlit side facing Earth. During a lunar eclipse, the Moon passes through Earth's shadow, so Earth blocks some or all of the direct sunlight that would otherwise reach it.
This distinction raises a question. If Earth is between the Sun and Moon near full Moon, why does an eclipse not occur every month? The Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbital plane. At most full Moons, the Moon passes above or below the central region of Earth's shadow instead of entering it.
The missing ingredient is a sufficiently precise alignment in space. An overpass and the road beneath it can seem to cross in a flat drawing even though they occupy different heights. Similarly, a simple flat diagram of the Sun, Earth, and Moon can hide the tilt that keeps the Moon outside the shadow.
Only when the Moon's position brings it into Earth's shadow near full Moon does a lunar eclipse occur. Full Moon is therefore a necessary condition for this event, but it does not by itself guarantee the event. The explanation depends on both the illuminated side we can see and the Moon's actual path through three-dimensional space.

questions.stimulusTitle: Charges That Need Room to Move
questions.stimulusText:
A crystal of ordinary table salt contains electrically charged particles called ions. Yet a solid salt crystal does not conduct an electric current in the way a salt solution can. The presence of charge is only part of the explanation. A current also requires charged particles that can travel through the material.
In the solid crystal, positive and negative ions are held in an orderly structure. They can vibrate around their positions, but they cannot move freely through the crystal. When the salt dissolves in water, the ions separate from that fixed arrangement and become mobile. Under an applied voltage, positive and negative ions move in opposite directions and carry current through the solution.
Melting salt also releases ions from the rigid solid arrangement. Thus, the important change is not the creation of charge from nothing. It is the availability of movement for charges that were already present.
Dissolving alone, however, is not enough to explain every solution. Sugar generally separates into neutral molecules when it dissolves. It does not provide the same abundant supply of mobile ions merely because it disappears from sight in water.
The examples distinguish three ideas that can easily be confused: being electrically charged, being able to move through a material, and being dissolved. To explain conduction, one must identify the particles and what they are free to do.

questions.stimulusText:
I used to believe I kept the building together. A finger touched one of my buttons, my doors closed, and I delivered people to the floor I had illuminated. Without me, surely, each floor would drift into a separate little world.
Then a maintenance worker fastened a notice to my doors: "Out of service until noon."
At first I enjoyed the importance of being unavailable. Footsteps approached, stopped, and retreated. Someone sighed. A young man with a large parcel settled down to wait nearby. This was encouraging. The building clearly needed me.
But other sounds traveled through the stairwell. A woman called a greeting upward. Two neighbors paused on a landing to compare the plants they were carrying. Someone laughed about having taken the wrong flight of stairs. The floors, to my considerable surprise, were continuing their conversations.
I began to suspect that I had confused carrying people with deciding where they belonged.
At noon the worker removed the notice. The young man stood, gathered his parcel, and pressed Five. I was pleased to be useful again. Yet the glowing number no longer looked quite like an order I had issued. It looked like a request I could answer.
I closed my doors and carried him upward. An elevator has a respectable job. Apparently, it need not also govern the building.

questions.stimulusText:
Animal body parts can be grouped in more than one useful way. If the question is which parts assist flight, a bird's wing and a butterfly's wing belong together. That group answers a question about function. It does not, by itself, show that the wings have the same internal construction.
A bird's wing contains upper-arm and forearm bones that correspond to bones in a human arm. Their proportions and uses differ, but their positions and connections reveal a shared structural pattern. A butterfly's wing does not contain that same forelimb arrangement. Thus, parts with different jobs can share a basic pattern, while parts with a similar job can be built differently.
Corresponding structures need not look identical. A bone may be lengthened, shortened, or differently shaped while retaining its place in an arrangement. Looking only at outward shape or at what a part does can therefore hide important anatomical relationships.
Neither grouping rule is useless. Someone studying the different ways animals fly may properly begin with function. Someone comparing underlying anatomy must ask about structures and connections instead. Claims about evolutionary relationships also require evidence beyond a single shared job. questions.prompt: What distinguishes the darkest region from the penumbra in this model?

choices.A: Only the darkest region contains an object.
choices.B: A different lamp lights the penumbra.
choices.C: All source light is blocked in the darkest region; only some is blocked in the penumbra.

questions.correctAnswer: All source light is blocked in the darkest region; only some is blocked in the penumbra.
questions.explanation: The model distinguishes complete blockage from partial blockage, where light from unblocked portions still reaches the surface.
questions.stimulusText:
A shadow need not have one sharp boundary. With a small, distant light source, its edge may look quite definite. With a larger source nearby, a broad gray region can appear between the darkest shadow and the fully lit surface.
To understand the difference, imagine several small lights spread across the face of one large lamp. Each casts a slightly displaced shadow of the same object. At some places, the object blocks light from every part of the source. These places form the darkest region. Elsewhere, the object blocks only some parts, while light from the remaining parts still reaches the surface.
The partly shaded region is called the penumbra. Moving across it changes how much of the source is visible, so the transition in brightness can be gradual rather than abrupt.
The explanation does not require the object itself to have a fuzzy edge. A sharply cut card can cast a soft-edged shadow when the lighting geometry creates a wide region of partial blockage. Changing the size or position of the source can change that region without changing the card.
The useful question is therefore not simply whether a surface is in shadow. One must also ask how much of the source is blocked there. A shadow records relationships among the source, object, and receiving surface.

choices.A: To give lamp assembly instructions
choices.B: To prove that all lamps contain separate bulbs
choices.C: To replace shadow observations with a lamp count
choices.D: To distinguish contributions from different positions and explain partial blockage

questions.correctAnswer: To distinguish contributions from different positions and explain partial blockage
questions.explanation: The imagined points clarify how some contributions are blocked while others arrive; the model is not a literal construction claim.
questions.stimulusText:
A shadow need not have one sharp boundary. With a small, distant light source, its edge may look quite definite. With a larger source nearby, a broad gray region can appear between the darkest shadow and the fully lit surface.
To understand the difference, imagine several small lights spread across the face of one large lamp. Each casts a slightly displaced shadow of the same object. At some places, the object blocks light from every part of the source. These places form the darkest region. Elsewhere, the object blocks only some parts, while light from the remaining parts still reaches the surface.
The partly shaded region is called the penumbra. Moving across it changes how much of the source is visible, so the transition in brightness can be gradual rather than abrupt.
The explanation does not require the object itself to have a fuzzy edge. A sharply cut card can cast a soft-edged shadow when the lighting geometry creates a wide region of partial blockage. Changing the size or position of the source can change that region without changing the card.
The useful question is therefore not simply whether a surface is in shadow. One must also ask how much of the source is blocked there. A shadow records relationships among the source, object, and receiving surface.

questions.skill: Main Idea, Central Thought, or Author's Purpose
questions.prompt: What distinction is central to the discussion?

choices.A: Every unanswered question makes a story meaningless.
choices.B: An action has no significance without dialogue.
choices.C: All predictions about an open ending are equally supported.
choices.D: An encounter can remain unresolved while a character’s changed attitude becomes clear.

questions.correctAnswer: An encounter can remain unresolved while a character’s changed attitude becomes clear.
questions.explanation: The essay separates uncertainty about the door’s answer from the visible attitude change expressed by choosing to knock.
questions.stimulusText:
Suppose a story follows a traveler returning to a house after a long disagreement with its occupants. Earlier, the traveler insists that carrying a key is enough: there will be no need to ask anyone for admission. In the final scene, the traveler reaches the door, puts the key away, and knocks. The story ends before anyone answers.
A reader may object that the ending leaves the most obvious question unresolved. Who opens the door, and what will happen next? Those questions remain open. Yet the story has answered another question: how the traveler now approaches the people inside. The gesture of knocking differs meaningfully from the earlier insistence on using the key.
Such an ending can withhold the outcome of an encounter while completing a change in attitude. Its lack of a final explanation need not mean that nothing has been achieved. The reader must identify which uncertainty remains and which development the last action makes visible.
Nor does an open ending make every interpretation equally persuasive. Predicting that the house will turn into a ship requires support this example has not supplied. An interpretation about changed expectations can point to the contrast between the key and the knock. An unfinished event still belongs to a shaped work, and a reader’s freedom remains connected to its evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is an interpretation about changed expectations stronger than the ship prediction?

choices.A: It invents more events.
choices.B: It connects the final gesture with the traveler’s earlier stated attitude.
choices.C: It depends on knowing the traveler’s name.
choices.D: It ignores the key and considers only the house’s size.

questions.correctAnswer: It connects the final gesture with the traveler’s earlier stated attitude.
questions.explanation: The contrast between using the key and knocking supplies textual evidence; the ship prediction has no comparable support.

choices.A: They show the traveler has forgotten how doors work.
choices.B: Their contrast makes a change in the traveler’s attitude visible through action.
choices.C: They identify who answers the door.
choices.D: They only establish the building’s size.

questions.explanation: The key initially expresses assumed entitlement, while knocking makes room for a response; the contrasting actions embody the change.
